For years the tech and entertainment industries have promised sound that surrounds us. Today every major platform supports Dolby Atmos, DTS:X, Sony 360 Reality Audio or some flavor of “spatial audio,” yet consumers get limited value from it. The technology works, argues the audio company Audioscenic; the value chain is broken, because the people who create, distribute and consume spatial content are disconnected by design.

Artists see no clear return. A good spatial mix can cost hundreds or thousands of dollars per song and needs a specialist studio and engineer. Apple appears to be the only service paying higher royalties for Atmos mixes, about 10% more, but at a reported $0.0076 per play the payoff is negligible, so spatial content stays confined to high-budget releases, often mixed remotely with little input from the artist. Listeners, meanwhile, mostly use phones, laptops, Bluetooth speakers and headphones, where spatial tracks fall back to stereo or to poor virtualization, so many cannot tell whether the feature is on. The same gap appears in film, streaming and even gaming, the strongest use case today.

The weakest link, the post concludes, is reproduction. Spatial audio will become valuable when everyday devices such as laptops, speakers, monitors and TVs deliver near-studio playback without setup. Audioscenic pitches its own technology here: listener-adaptive rendering that needs no calibration, only a listener seated in front of the device, as in the Razer Leviathan V2 Pro soundbar, which renders binaural audio over loudspeakers.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from a post on the Audioscenic blog. Read the original.
